paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The average person today buys sixty per cent more clothes than in 2000 but keeps each item for half as long. This pattern, known as fast fashion, relies on cheap production, rapidly changing styles and low prices. For consumers, it means constant novelty at little cost. For the environment, however, the price is high. I want to argue that responsibility lies with both shoppers and the industry, but that shoppers alone cannot solve the problem.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The fashion industry accounts for roughly ten per cent of global carbon emissions, more than international flights and shipping combined. It also uses vast amounts of water: producing one cotton T-shirt takes around 2,700 litres, equivalent to what a person drinks over two and a half years. Dyeing fabrics pollutes rivers in countries where regulation is weak, and synthetic materials such as polyester release tiny plastic fibres each time they are washed.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: What happens to clothes after use is equally worrying. In many countries, an item is thrown away after being worn only seven or eight times. Less than one per cent of clothing is recycled into new garments, because mixed fabrics are difficult to separate. Much donated clothing is shipped abroad, where it can overwhelm local markets and end up in landfill. It is therefore misleading to think that giving clothes to charity solves the problem.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Some commentators say that shoppers should simply buy less and choose better quality. This is sensible advice, and I follow it myself. But it places a burden on individuals who may not have the information or the money to do so. Ethical clothes are usually more expensive, and labels rarely explain a garment's environmental impact in a way people can compare. Moreover, the industry spends billions on advertising that encourages constant buying.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Real change requires regulation. France has banned the destruction of unsold clothing, and the European Union plans to make companies responsible for the waste their products create. Brands could also be required to publish information about the resources they use. Such measures would raise prices slightly, but they would reward companies that produce responsibly, and consumers could make real choices. Until then, wearing clothes for longer remains the most effective thing individuals can do.
